blocks.raw: <Tip>When a question presents a waste management scenario, apply the hierarchy in order: reduce (design changes, prefabrication), reuse (whole components), recycle (material streams), recover (energy), dispose (last resort). Do not assume all waste is recyclable; mixed materials, contaminated wood, and asbestos-containing products may only be landfilled after proper sorting. Always specify segregation methods and documented disposal destinations when answering waste management questions.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Confusing Waste Reduction with Recycling" severity="critical">Candidates often use "reduce" and "recycle" interchangeably. Reducing waste (source) is always preferable to recycling (end-of-life). If a prefabrication strategy eliminates 100 kg of concrete waste entirely, that is superior to generating 400 kg of waste and recycling 100 kg. Candidates must prioritize source reduction (design, prefab, lean construction) over end-of-life recycling in waste strategy recommendations.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Overestimating Recycling Rates in Philippines" severity="high">While developed countries recycle 30-50 percent of C&D waste, Philippines currently recycles less than 5 percent. Candidates cannot assume that segregated waste will be recycled; many municipalities lack facilities or markets for certain materials (contaminated wood, mixed gypsum). Strategies must account for realistic local recycling capacity: metals and rebar are high-value and recycled; concrete can be crushed for base course; wood is often landfilled or burned despite sustainability ideals.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Ignoring Contamination and Sorting Costs" severity="high">Candidates specify waste segregation without acknowledging that contaminated waste streams (sawdust mixed with concrete dust, adhesives on lumber, paint on drywall) cannot be easily recycled. Sorting labor and equipment costs may exceed material salvage value, making segregation economically infeasible. Candidates must recognize contamination risks and design strategies to prevent contamination at source (separate work areas, careful handling) rather than assuming end-of-life sorting is cost-effective.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw:
• Specifying waste reduction without identifying specific sources (e.g., 'reduce formwork waste' without addressing on-site concrete breakage or over-ordering)
  • Assuming 100% of segregated waste streams can find recycling or reuse markets; not accounting for market unavailability or contamination barriers
  • Calculating waste reduction percentages from prefabrication without baseline data; studies show 20-30% reduction, not 50%+ as optimistic assumptions suggest
  • Forgetting that RA 9003 waste management plans are mandatory for covered projects; omitting plan preparation violates environmental regulations
  • Proposing waste reduction strategies without cost-benefit analysis; most reduction methods (lean training, BIM quantification, prefab sourcing) require upfront investment
  • Ignoring that wood formwork and temporary structures account for much waste; candidates must address formwork reuse and design-for-reuse strategies
